questions.q: Lithium diethylcuprate, (C₂H₅)₂CuLi, is treated with iodomethane in dry ether. The alkane formed is:
questions.explain: One ethyl group of the cuprate couples with the methyl of CH₃I to give C₂H₅–CH₃ (propane); the second ethyl group is left behind as C₂H₅Cu.

questions.q: Which alkyl halide, used as R′–X with lithium dimethylcuprate, gives the poorest yield of the coupled alkane?
questions.explain: The coupling is an SN2-like backside attack, so methyl, primary, benzylic and allylic halides work well; a tertiary halide such as 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives poor yields or elimination.

questions.q: Why is the Corey–House synthesis preferred over the Wurtz reaction for preparing pentane?
options: Only the cross product R–R′ forms in significant amount, so an odd-carbon alkane is obtained cleanly
It needs no anhydrous conditions, unlike the Wurtz reaction
It works best with tertiary alkyl halides, which Wurtz cannot use
It uses sodium metal, which is cheaper than lithium
questions.explain: Wurtz with two different halides gives a mixture of R–R, R–R′ and R′–R′, whereas the cuprate couples selectively to R–R′. The cuprate is destroyed by water, so dry conditions are still essential.

questions.q: Which route is the best Corey–House plan for 2,2-dimethylbutane, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂CH₃?
questions.explain: The cuprate may carry a 3° group, but R′–X must be unhindered, so the tert-butyl part goes into the cuprate and the primary ethyl bromide is the halide. A 3° halide fails, Grignard reagents alone couple poorly, and the Wurtz mixture gives three alkanes.
